question: I've been working in Toronto for about 3 years. How much paid time off am I supposed to get each year?

Ontario.answer: At least two weeks of vacation each year (the two-week level applies to employees with less than five years of employment).
key_facts: At least 2 weeks of vacation

question: I've been at my job in Vancouver for six years now. Do I get any more vacation time than when I started?

British Columbia.answer: Yes. After five consecutive years of employment, the entitlement increases from at least two weeks to at least three weeks of annual vacation.
key_facts: At least 3 weeks of annual vacation
Up from at least 2 weeks before reaching 5 years
5 consecutive years of employment

question: I work in Ontario and have only been here for two years. How much vacation pay am I owed?

Ontario.answer: The employee is entitled to vacation pay of at least 4% of wages earned during the relevant period, excluding vacation pay.
key_facts: Minimum 4% vacation pay
Vacation pay is excluded from the wage calculation

question: What is the minimum vacation pay percentage for an Ontario employee with at least five years of employment?

Ontario.answer: The employee must receive vacation pay equal to at least 6% of wages earned during the relevant period, excluding vacation pay.
key_facts: Minimum 6% vacation pay
Vacation pay is excluded from the wage calculation

question: I work in Toronto and sometimes end up doing 48 hours a week. When should I start getting extra pay?

Ontario.answer: Overtime pay is required for hours worked beyond 44 in a work week (unless a different threshold is prescribed by regulation), at a minimum of 1.5 times the employee's regular rate.
key_facts: Weekly overtime threshold is 44 hours
Overtime rate is at least 1.5 times the regular rate

question: I just finished my first year working in BC. Am I supposed to get two weeks off now?

British Columbia.answer: Yes. After 12 consecutive months of employment, an employee is entitled to at least two weeks of annual vacation.
key_facts: At least 2 weeks of annual vacation

question: My boss in BC says my vacation pay will be lower this year because I got a bonus. Is that allowed?

British Columbia.answer: No. A BC employer must not reduce an employee's annual vacation or vacation pay because the employee was paid a bonus.
key_facts: Cannot reduce vacation or vacation pay because of a bonus

question: I'm working a 10-hour shift in BC today. Should the last couple of hours be paid at a higher rate?

British Columbia.answer: If the employee is not working under an averaging agreement, hours beyond eight in a day must be paid at 1.5 times the regular wage.
key_facts: Hours over 8 a day are paid at 1.5 times the regular wage
No averaging agreement applies

question: Can a BC employer use a single common date to calculate annual vacation entitlement for all of its employees?

British Columbia.answer: Yes. An employer may use a common date for calculating the annual vacation entitlement of all employees under sections 57 and 58, as long as this does not reduce any employee's rights under those sections.
key_facts: A common date for all employees is permitted
Must not reduce any employee's rights under those sections

question: What is the statutory deadline for paying vacation pay to a BC employee before their annual vacation begins?

British Columbia.answer: Vacation pay must be paid at least seven days before the beginning of the employee's annual vacation, unless it is paid on scheduled paydays under a written agreement or collective agreement.
key_facts: Payment at least 7 days before vacation
Or on scheduled paydays, if agreed in writing or provided by a collective agreement

question: I've worked at my job in Ottawa for 6 years. Would someone who's worked 6 years at a job in Vancouver get the same amount of vacation as me?

Ontario.answer: With five or more years of employment, an Ontario employee is entitled to at least three weeks of vacation.
key_facts: At least 3 weeks at 5 years or more

British Columbia.answer: After five consecutive years of employment, a BC employee is entitled to at least three weeks of annual vacation.
key_facts: At least 3 weeks after 5 consecutive years

comparison: Same: both at least 3 weeks after 5 years. Ontario ties it to completed vacation entitlement years; BC to consecutive years of employment.

question: Compare the deadline for an employee to take earned vacation in Ontario and British Columbia.

Ontario.answer: Vacation must be completed no later than 10 months after the end of the vacation entitlement year for which it is given.
key_facts: No later than 10 months after the end of the vacation entitlement year

British Columbia.answer: Annual vacation must be taken within 12 months after completing the year of employment that entitles the employee to it.
key_facts: Within 12 months after completing the entitling year of employment

comparison: Different: 10 months in Ontario vs. 12 months in BC.

question: We have staff in Toronto and Vancouver who'd rather bank their overtime and take time off later. Can we do that in both provinces, and do the rules differ?

Ontario.answer: Yes, if the employer and employee agree. The employee receives 1.5 hours of paid time off for each overtime hour, taken within 3 months of the work week in which it was earned (or within 12 months with the employee's agreement). If employment ends before the time off is taken, overtime pay is owed.
key_facts: Requires agreement between employer and employee
1.5 hours of paid time off per overtime hour
Taken within 3 months, or within 12 months with the employee's agreement
Paid out as overtime pay if employment ends first

British Columbia.answer: Yes. At the employee's written request, the employer may set up a time bank and credit overtime wages to it at overtime rates. The employee can ask at any time to be paid out, to use the credit for paid time off at an agreed time, or to close the bank. The employer may close it with one month's written notice and must settle it within 6 months. The balance must be paid on termination or when the employee asks to close it.
key_facts: Set up at the employee's written request
Overtime credited at overtime rates
Employee may request payout, time off, or closing at any time
Employer may close with 1 month's written notice and settle within 6 months
Balance paid on termination or on the employee's request to close

comparison: Different: both allow banking overtime, but Ontario uses an agreement with a 3- or 12-month deadline to take the time off, while BC uses a time bank set up at the employee's written request, with no use-by deadline stated while it is open.

question: We've got employees in Toronto and Vancouver who've both been here for six years. Do they get the same vacation pay percentage?

Ontario.answer: At least 6% of wages, excluding vacation pay, for employees with five or more years of employment.
key_facts: Minimum 6%
Excludes vacation pay from wages

British Columbia.answer: At least 6% of total wages during the relevant year after five consecutive years of employment.
key_facts: Minimum 6%
Based on total wages during the relevant year

comparison: Same: both at least 6% after five years. The wage base is worded differently (Ontario: wages excluding vacation pay earned in the period; BC: total wages in the entitling year).

question: If someone works 45 hours in a week, would they get overtime in Toronto and Vancouver, or does it depend on where they work?

Ontario.answer: Ontario's general weekly overtime threshold is 44 hours, so hours beyond 44 qualify for overtime at a minimum of 1.5 times the regular rate.
key_facts: 44-hour weekly threshold
At least 1.5 times the regular rate

British Columbia.answer: BC's weekly overtime threshold is 40 hours, with hours beyond 40 paid at 1.5 times the regular wage. Daily overtime also applies to any day over 8 hours.
key_facts: 40-hour weekly threshold
1.5 times the regular wage
Daily overtime may also apply for any day over 8 hours

comparison: Different: Ontario pays overtime only for the hour over 44. In BC overtime is owed, but whether it comes from the weekly rule (over 40) or the daily rule (over 8 a day) depends on how the hours fall across the days.

question: Compare the daily overtime rules in Ontario and BC for employees who work more than eight hours in a day.

Ontario.answer: Ontario's overtime section (s. 22) sets overtime on a weekly basis only: hours over 44 in a work week (or a prescribed threshold). It does not provide for daily overtime.
key_facts: No daily overtime threshold in s. 22

British Columbia.answer: BC requires 1.5 times regular wages for hours over eight in a day and double wages for hours over 12, unless an averaging agreement applies.
key_facts: Daily overtime after 8 hours
Double time after 12 hours
Averaging agreement may affect the calculation

comparison: Different: BC has daily overtime (1.5x over 8 hours, double over 12); Ontario has none, only a weekly threshold.

question: I want to split my vacation into single days instead of whole weeks. Can I do that in Ontario? What about in BC?

Ontario.answer: By default, Ontario vacation is taken in whole weeks (a two-week period or two one-week periods; for 5+ years, combinations of one-, two-, or three-week periods). Shorter periods are allowed only if the employee requests them in writing and the employer agrees.
key_facts: Default is whole-week periods
Shorter periods only if the employee requests in writing and the employer agrees

British Columbia.answer: BC requires the employer to allow an employee to take annual vacation in periods of one or more weeks. Section 57 does not address periods shorter than a week.
key_facts: Employer must allow vacation in periods of one or more weeks
Periods shorter than a week are not addressed in s. 57

comparison: Similar: both are built around whole weeks. Ontario allows shorter periods by written request plus employer agreement; BC requires the employer to allow periods of one week or more.

question: Compare the vacation pay payment-timing requirements in Ontario and BC.

Ontario.answer: Ontario requires vacation pay to be paid in a lump sum before the employee begins vacation by default. It may instead be paid each pay period if the employee agrees and the vacation pay is shown separately (other alternatives also exist, such as an agreed time).
key_facts: General rule is lump-sum payment before vacation
Payment during each pay period requires an agreement and separate identification of vacation pay

British Columbia.answer: BC requires vacation pay at least seven days before vacation begins, unless scheduled-payday payment is agreed to in writing or provided by a collective agreement.
key_facts: Payment at least 7 days before vacation
Or on scheduled paydays, if agreed in writing or provided by a collective agreement

comparison: Different: Ontario's default is a lump sum before vacation (with alternatives: payday, each pay period by agreement, or an agreed time); BC's default is at least 7 days before vacation, or on scheduled paydays if agreed in writing or by collective agreement.

question: Instead of getting my vacation pay all at once, can my employer in Ontario just add it to every paycheque?

Ontario.answer: Only if the employee has agreed to it and the vacation pay is shown separately, either on the wage statement for each pay period or on a separate statement given at the same time. Otherwise the default is a lump sum before the vacation starts.
key_facts: Requires an agreement between the employee and employer
Vacation pay shown separately on the wage statement, or on a separate statement provided at the same time
Default is a lump sum before vacation (s. 36(1))

question: How must an employer calculate vacation entitlement for an Ontario employee during a stub period created by an alternative vacation entitlement year?

Ontario.answer: The employer must calculate the ratio of the stub period to 12 months and apply it to the employee's applicable two-week or three-week vacation entitlement, using a separate calculation for employees without a regular work week.
key_facts: Calculate stub-period-to-12-month ratio
Less than 5 years: use 2 weeks as the base
5 years or more: use 3 weeks as the base
Employees without a regular work week use average weekly working days

question: My employer in Ontario wants to average my hours over a few weeks instead of paying overtime every time I go over 44 hours. Are they allowed to do that?

Ontario.answer: Yes, the employer and employee may agree to average hours over separate, non-overlapping, contiguous periods of two or more consecutive weeks, subject to the statutory requirements and a maximum of four weeks or the shorter period specified in the agreement.
key_facts: Employer and employee must agree
Periods must be separate, non-overlapping, and contiguous
Averaged over 2 to 4 weeks (or the shorter period specified in the agreement)
Agreement must have start and expiry dates
For non-union employees, the agreement expires no more than 2 years after the start date

question: What conditions must be met for a valid averaging agreement under BC's Employment Standards Act?

British Columbia.answer: The agreement must be written, signed by both parties before its start date, specify the averaging period and daily work schedule, and meet the other statutory requirements.
key_facts: Must be in writing
Must be signed before the start date
Must specify a 1-, 2-, 3-, or 4-week period
Must specify the daily work schedule
Employee must receive a copy before the averaging period begins

question: I work in Ontario and would rather take time off than get overtime pay. Can my employer let me do that?

Ontario.answer: Yes. The employer and employee may agree to paid time off at one and a half hours for each overtime hour worked. The time off must generally be taken within three months, or within 12 months if the employee agrees.
key_facts: Employer and employee must agree
1.5 hours of paid time off per overtime hour
Normally taken within 3 months
May be taken within 12 months with employee agreement

question: I started my job in Toronto on March 15, 2025. My manager says I have to use my vacation within 10 months of my vacation year ending. Can I save it and take it over the Christmas holidays this year (2026)?

Ontario.answer: Likely yes, timing-wise. Under the standard vacation entitlement year (which starts on the employee's first day of work), the first year ran March 15, 2025 to March 14, 2026. Vacation for that year must be completed within 10 months after it ends, so by about January 14, 2027, and December 2026 falls inside that window. However, the employer decides when vacation is taken, so the employee can request December but cannot insist. If the employer uses an alternative vacation entitlement year, the dates would be different.
key_facts: Deadline is 10 months after the end of the vacation entitlement year
Standard vacation entitlement year starts on the employee's first day of employment
First year ended March 14, 2026, so the deadline is about January 14, 2027
December 2026 is within the deadline
The employer determines when vacation is taken
Dates differ if the employer uses an alternative vacation entitlement year

question: I started a new job in BC last week. How long do I have to work before I'm entitled to vacation pay?

British Columbia.answer: An employee qualifies for at least 4% vacation pay after five calendar days of employment.
key_facts: 5 calendar days of employment
Minimum 4% vacation pay
Based on total wages during the relevant year

question: What are the daily and weekly overtime thresholds in BC for an employee who is not working under an averaging agreement?

British Columbia.answer: Daily overtime begins after eight hours, with double time after 12 hours. Weekly overtime begins after 40 hours, with only the first eight hours worked each day counted toward the weekly calculation.
key_facts: Daily threshold: 8 hours
Double-time threshold: 12 hours
Weekly threshold: 40 hours
Only first 8 hours per day count toward weekly overtime

British Columbia.answer: Cannot be determined from the Acts in the knowledge base.

question: My sister works in Calgary and I work in Toronto. We've both been at our jobs for 2 years. Do we get the same vacation pay?

Ontario.answer: An Ontario employee with less than five years of employment is entitled to vacation pay of at least 4% of wages, excluding vacation pay, earned during the relevant period.
key_facts: Minimum 4% vacation pay

British Columbia.answer: Cannot be determined from the Acts in the knowledge base. Section 40 sets the general overtime rules, but the BC Act's text does not address whether tech workers are excluded.
